bio.en: Gia Laudi (Georgiana Laudi) is the founder of the consultancy Forget The Funnel, where she works hands-on with SaaS companies to diagnose their biggest growth bottlenecks and frequently doubles or triples conversion across their product flows.
bio.zh: Gia Laudi（Georgiana Laudi）是咨询公司 Forget The Funnel 的创始人，她亲手帮助 SaaS 公司诊断最大的增长瓶颈，并常常将其产品流程中的转化率提升两到三倍。

summary.en: Gia makes the case that traditional funnels and pirate metrics like MQLs and SQLs are flawed because they put the business—not the customer—at the center and ignore everything that happens after acquisition, from retention to expansion. She shares the exact process she uses to find a company's biggest growth opportunities: identify your most important customers, map their journey through the product, set goals around their behavior, and then execute against those insights. A key point is that recurring-revenue businesses cannot treat growth as ending at acquisition, or they will not survive. The conversation is packed with practical tactics and stories about turning customer-centric diagnosis into measurable conversion wins.
summary.zh: Gia 指出，传统的漏斗模型以及 MQL、SQL 这类“海盗指标”是有问题的，因为它们把企业而非客户放在中心，并且完全忽略了获客之后发生的一切——从留存到扩展收入。她分享了自己在寻找公司最大增长机会时使用的完整流程：先锁定最重要的客户，再描绘他们在产品中的使用旅程，围绕他们的行为设定目标，然后基于这些洞察去执行。一个关键点是：订阅制营收的企业绝不能把增长当成“获客即结束”，否则就无法存活。整期内容充满了实战技巧和真实故事，教你如何把以客户为中心的诊断，转化为可衡量的转化提升。

turns.speaker: Georgiana Laudi
turns.en: The problem with funnels and pirate metrics and the favorites that I love to pick on are MQLs and SQLs is that nobody knows what those mean. It puts every customer in the same sort of buckets. It assumes that all customers and all products are the same. It puts businesses, or they, I should say, puts businesses at the center of the business versus putting customers at the center. Right? It's about the values of the business, not the value to the customer that's being measured. Also, it just kind of feels gross for people, this idea of pushing people through a funnel. And then probably a particularly relevant for SaaS companies is that recurring revenue businesses, you cannot think about marketing and growth and the business overall as ending an acquisition, otherwise you're not in business anymore. And the vast, vast majority of these models don't take post-acquisition, retention, expansion, all of that into account. So yeah, in a nutshell, funnels are bad.
turns.zh: 渠道和盗版指标以及我最喜欢选择的 MQL 和 SQL 的问题在于，没有人知道它们的含义。它将每个客户都放在同一类型的桶中。它假设所有客户和所有产品都是相同的。它将企业，或者我应该说，将企业置于业务的中心，而不是将客户置于中心。正确的？这是关于企业的价值，而不是所衡量的客户的价值。而且，这种将人们推向漏斗的想法对人们来说有点恶心。然后，可能与 SaaS 公司特别相关的是经常性收入业务，你不能将营销和增长以及整体业务视为结束收购，否则你就不再从事业务了。而且绝大多数这些模型都没有考虑收购后、保留、扩张，所有这些。所以，是的，简而言之，漏斗很糟糕。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Welcome to Lenny's Podcast. I'm Lenny, and my goal here is to help you get better at the craft of building and growing products. I interview world-class product leaders and growth experts to learn from their hard-won experiences building and scaling today's most successful companies. Today, my guest is Georgiana Laudi. Georgiana, aka Gia, runs a consultancy called Forget The Funnel, where she works hands on with SaaS companies to help them unlock and accelerate growth.
turns.zh: 欢迎来到莱尼的播客。我是莱尼，我的目标是帮助您更好地构建和种植产品。我采访了世界一流的产品领导者和增长专家，从他们建立和扩展当今最成功的公司的来之不易的经验中学习。今天，我的客人是乔治亚娜·劳迪。 Georgiana（又名 Gia）经营着一家名为 Forget The Funnel 的咨询公司，她与 SaaS 公司合作，帮助他们释放并加速增长。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: As you'll hear, she often finds huge unlocks and opportunities often doubling or tripling conversion in various points in their product flows. In our conversation, she shares the exact process that she goes through to help companies figure out where their biggest growth opportunities lie, and also how to execute on them. We chat about how to identify your most important customers, how to very practically map their journey through your flows and set goals, and then execute on your ideas. There's a lot of wisdom and some fun stories packed into this episode. So with that, I bring you Gia.
turns.zh: 正如您将听到的，她经常发现巨大的解锁和机会，通常可以使产品流中各个点的转化率增加一倍或三倍。在我们的谈话中，她分享了她帮助公司找出最大的增长机会所在以及如何执行这些机会的具体流程。我们讨论如何识别您最重要的客户，如何通过您的流程非常实际地规划他们的旅程并设定目标，然后执行您的想法。这一集充满了很多智慧和一些有趣的故事。因此，我给你带来了吉亚。

turns.zh: 我们一直认为 Amplitude 是支持整个产品循环、思考收集数据、通知投注、进行实验和学习。这就是我们成长的核心。令人惊奇的是，有多少客户正在使用 Amplitude 来分析实验、使用分段进行推广以及将数据发送到其他目的地。试验 CDP 源于倾听和观察客户的意见。

turns.zh: 支持成长和学习一直是 Amplitude 的核心重点，对吧？

turns.speaker: John Cutler
turns.en: Yeah. So Amplitude tries to meet customers where they are. We just launched Starter Templates and have a great scholarship program for startups. There's never been a more important time for growth.
turns.zh: 是的。因此，Amplitude 试图满足客户的需求。我们刚刚推出了入门模板，并为初创公司提供了很棒的奖学金计划。对于成长来说，从未有过如此重要的时刻。

turns.speaker: Lenny

turns.zh: 绝对同意。感谢您加入我们，约翰。前往振幅.com 开始。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Gia, welcome to the podcast.
turns.zh: Gia，欢迎来到播客。

turns.speaker: Georgiana Laudi
turns.en: Thanks so much for having me, Lenny.
turns.zh: 非常感谢你邀请我，莱尼。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's my pleasure. So we actually met over a decade ago, I think, maybe just around a decade in Montreal. I was working on my startup. You were helping companies with their websites, optimize their websites. Then you went on to lead marketing at Unbounce and a bunch of other great stuff. So just to set a little bit of foundation for listeners, can you talk about what you've done in your career in 55 seconds? That's your time box.
turns.zh: 这是我的荣幸。所以我想我们实际上是在十多年前认识的，也许就在蒙特利尔大约十年。我当时正在创业。您正在帮助公司建立网站，优化他们的网站。然后你继续领导 Unbounce 的营销工作以及其他一些很棒的工作。为了给听众打下基础，您能用 55 秒的时间谈谈您在职业生涯中做了什么吗？那是你的时间盒。

turns.speaker: Georgiana Laudi
turns.en: 55 seconds. Okay. So marketing for probably about 20 or so years, which sounds completely ridiculous when I say it, but I started working for my father's retail business in the early 2000s, probably 2000 actually. Worked there for a number of years, and then eventually left and started freelancing, worked at an agency. Terrible. And then actually probably around the time I met you, I had this little catalyst moment where I joined Twitter in late 2008, and I discovered the tech scene and startups. And that was, again, probably around the time that you and I met, maybe 2010 ish. And that was-
turns.zh: 55秒。好的。所以营销可能有大约 20 年左右的时间，当我这么说时听起来完全荒谬，但我在 2000 年代初开始为我父亲的零售业务工作，实际上可能是 2000 年。在那里工作了几年，然后最终离开并开始自由职业，在一家机构工作。糟糕的。实际上，大概就在我遇见你的时候，我在 2008 年底加入了 Twitter，发现了科技场景和初创公司。再说一次，那可能是你和我认识的时候，也许是 2010 年左右。那是——

turns.speaker: Georgiana Laudi
turns.en: And then I... What's that?
turns.zh: 然后我...那是什么？

turns.speaker: Georgiana Laudi
turns.en: 2011. See, there you go.

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Mm-hmm.
turns.zh: 嗯嗯。

turns.speaker: Georgiana Laudi
turns.en: So it was right around that time, and then late 2011, I decided supporting five, six companies at a time in their marketing and stuff like that. I was starting to get burnout, I was doing a lot, and I was like, "What would it feel like to sink my teeth into one brand?" So I decided to go in-house and I moved out west, and joined the team at Unbounce. I was there for five years. And then in late 2016, early 2017, I decided it was time to move on, and so I decided to go back independent and just started working with companies and supporting them through marketing and growth and product marketing. And that's what I've been doing ever since.
turns.zh: 所以就在那个时候，然后 2011 年末，我决定一次支持五、六家公司的营销和类似的事情。我开始精疲力尽，我做了很多事情，我想，“专注于一个品牌会是什么感觉？”所以我决定进入内部，然后搬到西部，加入了 Unbounce 的团队。我在那里待了五年。然后在 2016 年底、2017 年初，我决定是时候继续前进了，所以我决定重新独立，开始与公司合作，通过营销、增长和产品营销来支持他们。这就是我从那时起一直在做的事情。

turns.speaker: Georgiana Laudi
turns.en: But in mid 2017, I actually paired up with Claire Suellentrop who led marketing at Calendly, and her and I have been working together since about mid 2017. That's when we launched Forget The Funnel, and we started pairing up on working with companies and sort of married her customer research background in my strategy, marketing background. And we developed this framework that we now use when we work with predominantly B2B SaaS companies, is who we work with right now.
turns.zh: 但在 2017 年中期，我实际上与在 Calendly 负责营销的克莱尔·苏伦特罗普 (Claire Suellentrop) 合作，大约从 2017 年中期开始，我和她就开始合作。就在那时，我们推出了“忘记漏斗”(Forget The Funnel)，我们开始与公司合作，并将她的客户研究背景与我的战略、营销背景结合起来。我们开发了这个框架，现在我们与主要是 B2B SaaS 公司合作时使用该框架，这就是我们现在的合作伙伴。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. So we're going to spend a lot of time on what you've learned working with companies through Forget The Funnel. Why did you call it Forget The funnel?
turns.zh: 惊人的。因此，我们将花费大量时间来了解您通过“忘记漏斗”与公司合作所学到的知识。为什么你称其为“忘记漏斗”？

turns.speaker: Georgiana Laudi
turns.en: Because funnels are gross. I mean, it's a really antiquated idea. It's not just funnels that we sort of take issue with, it's buyers' journeys or even... I remember actually at Startup Fest 2012, I want to say, Dave McClure was talking about pirate metrics and I was like, "Huzzah, marketing has a role post acquisition. Everybody understands now." It was a real moment for me. But the problem with funnels and pirate metrics and the favorites that I love to pick on are MQLs and SQLs is that nobody knows what those mean. It puts every customer in the same sort of buckets. It assumes that all customers and all products are the same. It puts businesses, or they, I should say, puts businesses at the center of the business versus putting customers at the center. It's about the values of the business, not the value to the customer that's being measured.
turns.zh: 因为漏斗很恶心。我的意思是，这是一个非常过时的想法。我们所质疑的不仅仅是渠道，还有买家的旅程，甚至……我实际上记得在 2012 年创业节上，我想说，戴夫·麦克卢尔 (Dave McClure) 正在谈论盗版指标，我当时想，“哈扎，营销在收购后发挥着作用。现在每个人都明白了。”这对我来说是一个真正的时刻。但渠道和盗版指标以及我最喜欢选择的 MQL 和 SQL 的问题在于，没有人知道它们的含义。它将每个客户都放在同一类型的桶中。它假设所有客户和所有产品都是相同的。它将企业，或者我应该说，将企业置于业务的中心，而不是将客户置于中心。这是关于企业的价值，而不是所衡量的客户的价值。

turns.speaker: Georgiana Laudi
turns.en: Also, it just kind of feels gross for people, this idea of pushing people through a funnel. And then probably a particularly relevant for SaaS companies is that recurring revenue businesses, you cannot think about marketing and growth and the business overall as ending at acquisition. Otherwise, you're not in business anymore. The vast, vast majority of these models don't take post-acquisition retention, expansion, all of that into account. They also leave the problem stage out. So the world that customers are living in prior to discovering you, which is a really critical, that context is unbelievably valuable, especially for marketing. So to delete that out of the equation is a big problem. So yeah, in a nutshell, funnels are bad.
turns.zh: 而且，这种将人们推向漏斗的想法对人们来说有点恶心。对于 SaaS 公司来说，可能特别相关的是经常性收入业务，你不能将营销和增长以及整体业务视为以收购结束。否则，你就不再做生意了。这些模型中的绝大多数都没有考虑收购后的保留、扩张，所有这些。他们也将问题阶段排除在外。因此，客户在发现您之前所生活的世界非常关键，这种背景非常有价值，尤其是对于营销而言。因此，将其从等式中删除是一个大问题。所以，是的，简而言之，漏斗很糟糕。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So I'm excited to dig into a lot of stuff you've learned, but I have a couple other things I just wanted to talk about to set the foundation.
turns.zh: 好的。所以我很高兴能深入研究你们学到的很多东西，但我还有一些其他的事情想谈谈来奠定基础。

turns.speaker: Georgiana Laudi
turns.en: Mm-hmm.
turns.zh: 嗯嗯。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: One is, can you talk about some of the impact that you've seen working with companies through the process that you've come up with? What kind of impact have you seen? What kind of numbers have you seen?
turns.zh: 一是，您能谈谈您在与公司合作过程中所看到的一些影响吗？您看到了什么样的影响？你见过什么样的数字？

turns.speaker: Georgiana Laudi
turns.en: I would say, far in a way the biggest, most immediate impact of the type of work that we do is realigning with that ideal customer. Generally, the lowest hanging fruit outcome is realigning around better positioning and messaging. And identifying more resonant positioning and messaging that speaks to that context that I was talking about before, before people discover that you even exist, have that moment where they're like, "Oh my god, this has to change. This sucks," ties that in, ties in what they care about and what is valuable about your product and then also that desired outcome. I mean, for those in the know, jobs to be done is a big sort of influence here, but if you can identify that type of information about your customers and get to know them at that level, then you are in a way better position to be able to not only position your product but also use much more powerful messaging.
turns.zh: 我想说，在某种程度上，我们所做的工作类型最大、最直接的影响就是与理想客户重新协调。一般来说，最容易实现的结果是围绕更好的定位和信息传递进行重新调整。在人们发现你的存在之前，确定更能引起共鸣的定位和信息，与我之前谈论的背景相关联，让他们有这样的时刻，“天哪，这必须改变。这太糟糕了”，将他们关心的东西和你的产品的价值以及期望的结果联系起来。我的意思是，对于那些了解情况的人来说，要做的工作在这里有很大的影响，但如果你能够识别有关你的客户的此类信息并在那个级别上了解他们，那么你就处于一个更好的位置，不仅能够定位你的产品，而且还能够使用更强大的消息传递。

turns.speaker: Georgiana Laudi
turns.en: So typically, what we do is, we'll identify those gaps of almost, I mean I shouldn't even say nine times out of 10, 99 times out of a hundred, a company's website is not doing as much as it could do. It's not being as effective from a messaging and positioning standpoint as it could. So websites tend to get update. We will do a lot of overhauls on messaging on a website and improve performance there. One of my favorite examples of that is a social media tool that we worked with where we did really very simple research for them, honestly, identified two different jobs to be done, zeroed in on one of them, and then updated the messaging on the website.
turns.zh: 因此，通常情况下，我们所做的是，我们会找出这些差距，我的意思是我什至不应该说十之九、一百之九十九，一家公司的网站没有尽其所能。从消息传递和定位的角度来看，它并没有达到应有的效果。所以网站往往会更新。我们将对网站上的消息传递进行大量修改并提高其性能。我最喜欢的例子之一是我们使用的社交媒体工具，我们为他们做了非常简单的研究，老实说，确定了两项不同的工作要做，专注于其中一项，然后更新网站上的消息。

turns.speaker: Georgiana Laudi
turns.en: We shortened the trial from 30 days to seven. The conversion on the website went up with this new messaging by 89%. But the thing that I love the most about that particular story is that we didn't even touch anything after the signup experience. We hadn't even gotten there and the trial-to-paid conversion rate increased 40%, and we didn't touch it. It was just because a more qualified, better fit customer was coming through the door. So there was more of them and there were better qualified. So that's a really specific example that is very typical of this type of work.
turns.zh: 我们将试用期从 30 天缩短到 7 天。这条新消息使网站转化率提高了 89%。但我最喜欢这个特定故事的一点是，在注册体验之后我们甚至没有碰过任何东西。我们甚至还没有达到这个目标，试用到付费的转化率增加了 40%，但我们没有触及它。这只是因为一个更合格、更适合的客户进来了。因此，他们的人数更多，资质也更好。这是一个非常具体的例子，是此类工作中非常典型的。

turns.speaker: Georgiana Laudi
turns.en: There's other examples, though, of product adoption and using that messaging and positioning past the website, even in the product onboarding itself, email and app, whatever, and just making sure that they're getting to and have the calms to get to the parts of the product that they care about the most, which can increase trial-to-paid or product activation. With Autobooks, the product usage of the North Star product usage jumped by 300% or something within quite a short period of time after rolling out email onboarding to support that product experience. I know SparkToro as well, which I think we might end up talking about again when we talk about the process, they doubled their trial-to-paid conversion rate when we worked with them because of post acquisition optimization to their messaging.
turns.zh: 不过，还有其他产品采用的例子，以及通过网站使用该消息传递和定位，甚至在产品入门本身、电子邮件和应用程序等方面，只要确保他们能够并平静地接触他们最关心的产品部分，这可以增加试用付费或产品激活。借助 Autobooks，在推出电子邮件引导以支持产品体验后，North Star 产品的使用量在相当短的时间内跃升了 300% 左右。我也了解 SparkToro，我认为当我们谈论流程时，我们最终可能会再次谈论它，当我们与他们合作时，由于对其消息传递进行了收购后优化，他们的试用到付费转化率翻了一番。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I imagine people are listening to this and they're like, "This is what I'm waiting for, some kind of huge win, some huge conversion, a success." I'm curious, how often do you find companies have something like this, like a latent opportunity to double, triple conversion? Everyone's hoping a conversion like this.
turns.zh: 我想人们听到这个之后会想，“这就是我在等待的，某种巨大的胜利，某种巨大的转变，一种成功。”我很好奇，你多久发现公司有这样的事情，比如双倍、三倍转化的潜在机会？每个人都希望有这样的转变。

turns.speaker: Georgiana Laudi
turns.en: Oh, boy.
turns.zh: 哦，男孩。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. What's the general hit rate?
turns.zh: 是的。一般命中率是多少？

turns.speaker: Georgiana Laudi
turns.en: So many. I mean I would say, pretty well every company we've ever worked with has... Not pretty well. Every company we've ever worked with has learned something new about their customers that they can apply at some juncture of their customer's experience, whether or not it is in campaigns to reach the right people out in the world, whether or not it's doing a better job with their messaging and positioning on their website, or their go-to market or acquisition strategy on their website using a sandbox account or getting a faux freemium account to let people kick the tires of their product prior to getting on a sales call. That's something that could potentially happen.
turns.zh: 这么多。我的意思是，我想说，我们合作过的每家公司都……不太好。我们合作过的每家公司都从他们的客户中学到了一些新的东西，他们可以在客户体验的某个时刻应用这些东西，无论是在营销活动中接触到世界上合适的人，无论是在他们的网站上更好地传达信息和定位，还是在他们的网站上使用沙盒帐户或获得虚假免费增值帐户让人们在接到销售电话之前先试用他们的产品，以进入市场或获取策略。这是有可能发生的事情。

turns.speaker: Georgiana Laudi
turns.en: The post-acquisition experience I'm talking about, it is so often an afterthought somehow where that additional of layer... I think part of the reason why it's an afterthought is because product onboarding in particular, and you've probably heard this too, it tends to be kind of like no man's land. Who owns that? Is it marketing? If it's freemium, in my opinion it should be marketing because freemium is a marketing tool, but not everybody subscribes to that. Not every company would necessarily agree that that's the case. A lot of companies might say, "No, it's product." So we end up seeing a messy middle there because there's no natural handoff. So pretty well, every company that we've worked with has had an opportunity to improve, especially product onboarding and product activation.
turns.zh: 我所说的收购后体验，通常是事后的想法，其中附加的层……我认为这是事后的部分原因是因为特别是产品入职，你可能也听说过，它往往有点像无人区。谁拥有它？是营销吗？如果是免费增值，我认为它应该是营销，因为免费增值是一种营销工具，但并不是每个人都认同这一点。并非每家公司都一定同意这种情况。很多公司可能会说：“不，这是产品。”所以我们最终会看到中间很混乱，因为没有自然的切换。非常好，我们合作过的每家公司都有机会改进，特别是产品入门和产品激活。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. So basically everybody will benefit from what we're about to talk about.
turns.zh: 惊人的。所以基本上每个人都会从我们即将讨论的内容中受益。

turns.speaker: Georgiana Laudi
turns.en: A hundred percent.
turns.zh: 百分之一百。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Great.
turns.zh: 惊人的。伟大的。

turns.speaker: Georgiana Laudi
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: All right. We've got wrap detention as a way to maybe transition into your process. So you're visiting a site once, and I invited you to the Airbnb office we were having a happy hour, and I gave you a tour. You told me later that something you saw while you're walking around the office transformed the way you think about growth and inform the way you think about approaching this problem. Can you talk about that?
turns.zh: 好的。我们有包裹拘留作为可能过渡到您的流程的一种方式。你曾经访问过一个网站，我邀请你到 Airbnb 办公室，我们正在享受欢乐时光，我还带你参观了一下。你后来告诉我，你在办公室走来走去时看到的一些东西改变了你对增长的看法，并告诉你如何解决这个问题。你能谈谈吗？

turns.speaker: Georgiana Laudi
turns.en: Yes. This is one of my favorite... It was 2013, so you and I might have met in 2011, and then a couple years later I was in town for a conference and we toured the office, HQ and everything. Of course, it was all stars in my eyes because what a beautiful office too. So it was quite like, I would've remembered it regardless. But we went downstairs, very different from the very polished upstairs. We went downstairs to where your working area was, where the product team was, and there were sheets of paper taped to the wall, a bunch in a row. And it would've been easy to miss because it's kind of chaotic down there, but it was the customer journey of an Airbnb customer through two posts.
turns.zh: 是的。这是我最喜欢的之一……那是 2013 年，所以你和我可能在 2011 年见过面，几年后我在城里参加一个会议，我们参观了办公室、总部和一切。当然，我眼中都是星星，因为办公室也很漂亮。所以就像是，无论如何我都会记住它。但我们下了楼，与楼上的光鲜亮丽的很不一样。我们下楼到你们的工作区、产品团队所在的地方，墙上贴着几张纸，一排排的。这很容易被错过，因为那里有点混乱，但这是 Airbnb 客户通过两个帖子的客户旅程。

turns.speaker: Georgiana Laudi
turns.en: What struck me, I was like, "Oh that's interesting. I'm in the middle of building one out for us." Leading marketing at Unbounce at the time. And I was interestingly with the customer success, he was also with me. So Ryan Engley was there with me, and it was the perfect sort of that him and I saw it together. It was a customer journey that was focused on the customer. So versus that pirate metrics problem or that the typical buyer's journey problem that I was talking about earlier, it was the complete reverse of that. It was illustrated. The emotional journey was part of it. The role that Airbnb played as a direct touchpoint and also indirect, what was going on in the person's life that had nothing to do outside of Airbnb, which I thought was really interesting.
turns.zh: 让我震惊的是，我当时想，“哦，这很有趣。我正在为我们建造一个。”当时在 Unbounce 负责营销工作。有趣的是，我对客户的成功很感兴趣，他也和我在一起。所以瑞恩·恩格利和我在一起，他和我一起看到了这一切，这是完美的。这是一个以客户为中心的客户旅程。因此，与我之前讨论的盗版指标问题或典型的买家旅程问题相比，情况完全相反。对此进行了说明。情感之旅是其中的一部分。 Airbnb 扮演了一个直接接触点和间接接触点的角色，人们的生活中发生了一些与 Airbnb 无关的事情，我认为这非常有趣。

turns.speaker: Georgiana Laudi
turns.en: It was like, the beautiful little milestones really encapsulated in a sort of snapshot way, such that anybody walking by it or anybody being reminded that it existed could understand in a glance what the goal was at each of those milestones. I was like, "Well, shit, this is completely through the lens of the customer versus the business and the grossness of the funnel." It's just so far removed from that experience that I was like, "Ryan, look at this. We need this." He was like, "Oh yeah, this is good." I took a picture. Can't find it for the life of me.
turns.zh: 就像，美丽的小里程碑确实以一种快照的方式封装起来，这样任何走过它的人或任何被提醒它存在的人都可以一眼就明白每个里程碑的目标是什么。我当时想，“好吧，该死，这完全是通过客户与业务以及渠道的粗糙性来看待的。”这与那种经历相去甚远，我当时想，“瑞安，看看这个。我们需要这个。”他说：“哦，是的，这很好。”我拍了一张照片。我找了一辈子都找不到。

turns.speaker: Georgiana Laudi
turns.en: But we returned back to the office the following week, and co-founder and head of product, head of CS, so Ryan, Carter Gilchrist, who's head of product and co-founder, Ryan, and I, head of marketing, the three of us locked ourselves in the room for two days and made our own. It was a circle. I mean looking back, it's hysterical, but it was sort of democratized to the rest of the team in a way because it had that buy-in. Everybody was like, "Oh yeah. Okay, this makes sense and I understand." It made everybody feel a lot better about what they were doing because it was about value, delivering value at each of the points.
turns.zh: 但我们在接下来的一周回到了办公室，联合创始人兼产品主管、CS 主管，所以 Ryan、产品主管兼联合创始人 Carter Gilchrist、Ryan 和我，营销主管，我们三个人把自己锁在房间里两天，自己做了。这是一个圆圈。我的意思是回想起来，这有点歇斯底里，但在某种程度上，它对团队其他成员来说是民主化的，因为它得到了支持。每个人都说，“哦，是的。好吧，这是有道理的，我明白。”这让每个人都对自己所做的事情感觉好多了，因为这关乎价值，在每个点上交付价值。

turns.speaker: Georgiana Laudi
turns.en: So that grossness sort of goes away and we're like, "Oh cool." I don't want to be too kumbaya about it, but it was a bit of a moment. And also, it made communicating with especially the product team and the engineering team a lot easier for me. So we were using a shared language. The rest of the company who aren't necessarily customer facing really understood, I think, at a different level what we were all doing together in KPIs, yada yada yada. So it was amazing. Honestly, I mean I can't credit only that obviously to our growth, but it was a pretty impressive couple years that followed that. I think the alignment that that brought us was huge. Yeah. Anyway, that's the story. Sorry, that wasn't super short, but it was big.
turns.zh: 这样，那种粗俗感就消失了，我们会说，“哦，太酷了。”我不想对此太过愤怒，但这确实是一个时刻。而且，它使我与产品团队和工程团队的沟通变得更加容易。所以我们使用共同的语言。我认为，公司其他不一定面向客户的人员在不同层面上真正理解我们在 KPI 中共同所做的事情，yada yada yada。所以这太棒了。老实说，我的意思是我不能仅仅将这一点归功于我们的增长，但随后的几年是令人印象深刻的。我认为这给我们带来了巨大的一致性。是的。无论如何，这就是故事。抱歉，那不是很短，但很大。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's great.
turns.zh: 那太棒了。

turns.speaker: Georgiana Laudi
turns.en: It was a big thing. Yeah.
turns.zh: 这是一件大事。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We're going to link pictures of this on the show notes. Internally, it was called Project Snow White because it was inspired by-
turns.zh: 我们将在演出笔记中链接此图片。在内部，它被称为“白雪公主计划”，因为它的灵感来自-

turns.speaker: Georgiana Laudi
turns.en: Oh yeah, that's right.
turns.zh: 哦，是的，没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. It was inspired by Brian reading the biography of Walt Disney, and they needed to create the storyboard basically to create Snow White because it was so complicated to make that movie. It might have been the first animated film with storyboards.
turns.zh: 是的。它的灵感来自于布莱恩阅读华特·迪士尼传记，他们基本上需要创建故事板来创作白雪公主，因为制作那部电影非常复杂。这可能是第一部带有故事板的动画电影。

turns.speaker: Georgiana Laudi
turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So it was basically a storyboard of a trip on Airbnb of a host and a guest.
turns.zh: 所以它基本上是一个房东和房客在 Airbnb 上旅行的故事板。

turns.speaker: Georgiana Laudi
turns.en: That's right.
turns.zh: 这是正确的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And in detail, I forget if I told you this, but Airbnb hired a full-time storyboard artist from Pixar to draw these key frames.
turns.zh: 具体来说，我忘了我是否告诉过你这一点，但 Airbnb 聘请了皮克斯的全职故事板艺术家来绘制这些关键帧。

turns.speaker: Georgiana Laudi
turns.en: I think I did know that. I was very grateful to have seen it. I didn't realize at the time, but it changed the way, like you said at the beginning, it changed the way that I thought about marketing because it really made it obvious to not only me, of course, and to everybody, that customer experience layer, that marketers are so good at, has such an incredibly important role in driving revenue. Not just in building awareness, but in playing a major role in helping customers get value and catching them when they fall off and all that kind of stuff. So it changed a lot for us.
turns.zh: 我想我确实知道这一点。我很感激能看到它。我当时没有意识到，但它改变了方式，就像你一开始说的那样，它改变了我对营销的思考方式，因为它确实不仅对我来说，而且对每个人来说都显而易见，营销人员所擅长的客户体验层在推动收入方面具有非常重要的作用。不仅是在建立意识方面，而且在帮助客户获得价值并在他们摔倒时接住他们等方面发挥重要作用。所以这对我们来说改变了很多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And it informed the way that you approach your consultancy with Forget The funnel. So as a transition to talk about that, the way I'm thinking we approach this is, imagine a customer, what is the process you go through? What are the steps? How do you go about helping a company figure out where they should invest, what they're doing right and wrong? I should also mention you're writing a book about this that's going to explain this whole process, that's coming out later in the year.
turns.zh: 它告诉你如何通过忘记漏斗来进行咨询。因此，作为谈论这个问题的过渡，我认为我们处理这个问题的方式是，想象一下客户，您经历的流程是什么？步骤是什么？你如何帮助公司弄清楚他们应该在哪里投资，他们的做法正确和错误？我还应该提到您正在写一本关于此的书，该书将解释整个过程，该书将于今年晚些时候出版。

turns.speaker: Georgiana Laudi
turns.en: Right. Yeah.
turns.zh: 正确的。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So we'll talk about that at the end as well. I'll turn over to you.
turns.zh: 所以我们也会在最后讨论这个问题。我会交给你。

turns.speaker: Georgiana Laudi
turns.en: Cool. I mean if I go down a rabbit hole and you want to pull me out and have me unpack something, let me know. Well, the process is pretty straightforward. At the highest level, the idea is, understand your best customers, map their experience, like we were just talking about, map their experience through the lens of delivering value to them, make it measurable, and then evaluate what you're doing today that is out of alignment with that. Pretty straightforward. I mean that doesn't sound too hard of a job, of course. But research is an really important part of that. So the story that I was going to use to illustrate this is, there's a company that we work with from time to time. We worked with them at least twice, arguably three times.
turns.zh: 凉爽的。我的意思是，如果我掉进了兔子洞，而你想把我拉出来并让我打开一些东西，请告诉我。嗯，这个过程非常简单。在最高层面上，我们的想法是，了解你最好的客户，绘制他们的体验，就像我们刚才讨论的那样，通过向他们提供价值的角度绘制他们的体验，使其可衡量，然后评估你今天所做的与此不相符的事情。非常简单。当然，我的意思是，这听起来并不是一项太难的工作。但研究是其中非常重要的一部分。所以我要用这个故事来说明这一点，我们不时与一家公司合作。我们与他们合作了至少两次，可以说是三次。

turns.speaker: Georgiana Laudi
turns.en: So Rand Fishkin who was the founder of Moz, he's got a new product. It's an audience research tool called SparkToro. And when they first launched, actually even pre-launched, Rand and Casey came to Claire and I to help with their positioning and messaging as they were going forward to launch. I mean Rand and Casey, they're both very, very thoughtful and they take their time with stuff. So they were just looking for that extra layer of like, "Is this good enough to launch kind of thing?" So we help them with their positioning and messaging. And off they went.
turns.zh: Moz 的创始人兰德·菲什金 (Rand Fishkin) 推出了一款新产品。这是一个名为 SparkToro 的受众研究工具。当他们第一次推出时，实际上甚至是预先推出时，兰德和凯西来找克莱尔和我，帮助他们在即将推出时进行定位和传达信息。我的意思是兰德和凯西，他们都非常非常体贴，而且他们花时间做事。所以他们只是在寻找额外的一层，比如“这是否足以推出某种东西？”因此，我们帮助他们定位和传达信息。他们就出发了。

turns.speaker: Georgiana Laudi
turns.en: About a year later, they came back because though they were doing a decent job generating traffic and interest in SparkToro, I mean Rand is no small fish so he's got a good audience built in, which is fantastic, but those that were getting to the website... Those that were signing up for the product, those weren't issues. But the people that were signing up for their free product weren't converting to paid in the way that they believed they could. So we decided to work with them and basically go to the source and find out, from SparkToro's best customers, what can we learn from them that we can then reflect back in the product experience and the customer experience for them?
turns.zh: 大约一年后，他们回来了，因为尽管他们在为 SparkToro 带来流量和兴趣方面做得不错，但我的意思是 Rand 不是小鱼，所以他内置了很好的受众，这太棒了，但那些访问该网站的人……那些注册该产品的人，这些都不是问题。但那些注册免费产品的人并没有像他们认为的那样转变为付费产品。因此，我们决定与他们合作，基本上从 SparkToro 的最佳客户那里找出源头，我们可以从他们那里学到什么，然后我们可以反映在他们的产品体验和客户体验中？

turns.speaker: Georgiana Laudi
turns.en: So I mentioned it before, but we are heavy believers in the jobs-to-be-done theory, which is basically this idea that people don't buy your product, they buy the better version of themselves, yada yada. I don't need to explain any of that. But we use that to guide our research. And with SparkToro, we were in a position, and the purists will hate me saying this, but we were in a position to be able to run surveys. So yes, interviews are ideal always, but we did think that we could learn a ton from surveys to then, if needed, double down with interviews. We didn't end up actually needing to run the interviews because the surface that we ran were pretty decisive and clear in terms of what we learned. So what we did was, we identified SparkToro's best customers. Now, what I mean by best customers is those that get a ton of value from your product as of exist today, pay obviously. They're happy. They're low maintenance. And very importantly, they signed up for your product recently enough that they remember what life was like before.
turns.zh: 所以我之前提到过，但我们是待完成工作理论的坚定信徒，这基本上是这样的想法：人们不会购买你的产品，他们会购买更好的自己版本，yada yada。我不需要解释任何这些。但我们用它来指导我们的研究。通过 SparkToro，我们处于一个有利的位置，纯粹主义者会讨厌我这么说，但我们处于能够进行调查的位置。所以，是的，采访总是理想的，但我们确实认为我们可以从调查中学到很多东西，然后，如果需要的话，可以加倍采访。我们最终实际上并不需要进行采访，因为就我们所了解到的情况而言，我们进行的表面相当明确且清晰。所以我们所做的是，我们确定了 SparkToro 的最佳客户。现在，我所说的最佳客户是那些从你的产品中获得大量价值的客户，他们显然会付费。他们很高兴。它们的维护成本低。非常重要的是，他们最近注册了你的产品，以至于他们记得以前的生活是什么样的。

turns.speaker: Georgiana Laudi
turns.en: So generally, we say that's in the three to six-month range. Because if you go to somebody that's been your customer for two years, they're just going to fill answers with what they think might have been going on in their life. But if you ask customers who remember what life was like before, you're going to get a lot more interesting responses, a lot more accurate depiction of what was going on. So that's the criteria we went forward. Surveyed their customers. We're trying to uncover from them what was going on in their life when they were seeking out a solution, what happened, what was that trigger moment when they did start seeking a solution, what did they go to, who did they talk with, what were their influences? Which PS, that's what SparkToro does, it helps you identify those.
turns.zh: 一般来说，我们说的是三到六个月的范围。因为如果你去找一个已经是你两年客户的人，他们只会用他们认为生活中可能发生的事情来填写答案。但如果你问那些记得以前生活是什么样子的顾客，你会得到更有趣的回答，对正在发生的事情有更准确的描述。这就是我们前进的标准。调查了他们的客户。我们试图向他们揭示当他们寻求解决方案时他们的生活中发生了什么，发生了什么，当他们开始寻求解决方案时的触发时刻是什么，他们去了哪里，他们与谁交谈，他们的影响是什么？其中 PS，这就是 SparkToro 所做的，它可以帮助您识别这些。

turns.speaker: Georgiana Laudi
turns.en: But also, what were they looking for in a solution? What were the must-haves for them versus what were some of the anxieties that they had, some deal breakers, things like that? So basically unpacking what is it that was critical for them in their solution. And then of course, what is it they're able to do now that they weren't able to do before. So that desired outcome. So out of that, we identified a couple of different options, a couple of different jobs, customer jobs, and we have to prioritize one, of course, because if you start right off the bat with like, "Okay, we're going to solve for all of these different customers jobs," then you end up not being as resonant. You can't be as effective. So we focused in on one.
turns.zh: 而且，他们在解决方案中寻找什么？他们必须拥有什么，而他们有哪些焦虑，一些破坏交易的事情，诸如此类的事情？所以基本上解开他们的解决方案中对他们来说至关重要的是什么。当然，他们现在能够做哪些以前无法做到的事情。这样就达到了想要的结果。因此，我们确定了几种不同的选择，几种不同的工作，客户工作，当然，我们必须优先考虑其中一个，因为如果你一开始就说，“好吧，我们将解决所有这些不同客户的工作”，那么你最终不会引起共鸣。你不可能那么有效。所以我们专注于其中之一。

turns.speaker: Georgiana Laudi
turns.en: And the way that you make a decision on which one you focus on is similar to best customers. So high willingness to pay. There's no question whether or not they would pay for a product like yours. The handholding that they would need would be minor or less so. And I say that understanding full well the difference between product-led and sales-led. I'm not saying that sales-led is not good, but sometimes there's a decision to be made. If you're not set up today to support a sales-led or high touch, then you may want to opt for the more product-led approach. And the reverse is also true if you've got a robust sales team, well then, you might actually be better off leveraging sales more in that scenario and might want to attend towards that. But there's that criteria that you would think through.
turns.zh: 您决定关注哪个客户的方式与最佳客户类似。支付意愿如此之高。毫无疑问，他们是否愿意为像您这样的产品付费。他们所需要的帮助将是次要的或更少的。我说要充分理解以产品为主导和以销售为主导之间的区别。我并不是说以销售为主导不好，但有时需要做出决定。如果您现在还没有准备好支持以销售为主导的或高接触的方式，那么您可能需要选择更多以产品为主导的方法。反之亦然，如果您拥有一支强大的销售团队，那么，在这种情况下，您实际上可能会更好地利用销售，并且可能希望参与其中。但你需要考虑这个标准。

turns.speaker: Georgiana Laudi
turns.en: So willingness to pay, it's really obvious. Maybe the most important one is that they have an urgent problem. So the whole pain killer versus vitamin thing, you always want to be selling a pain killer. So who has an urgent problem that needs solving, not something that they might have a problem with six months down the line? Who has a high retention or even expansion potential is also really advantageous for very obvious reasons. So customers who would have a long-term need for this type of product and even potentially have that need expand or change over time and evolve in ways that you envision the product can help them.
turns.zh: 所以付费意愿，真的很明显。也许最重要的是他们有一个紧迫的问题。因此，在止痛药与维生素的比较中，你总是想销售止痛药。那么谁有一个需要解决的紧急问题，而不是六个月后可能出现的问题呢？出于非常明显的原因，具有高保留甚至扩展潜力的人也确实具有优势。因此，对此类产品有长期需求，甚至可能有这种需求的客户会随着时间的推移而扩展或改变，并以您设想的产品可以帮助他们的方式发展。

turns.speaker: Georgiana Laudi
turns.en: And then there's other criteria too. So sometimes you might want to prioritize one customer job over another, if those customers congregate in a way that make them really easy to market to. That's an advantage. Or another advantage, and this was the case for SparkToro, is you have an unfair advantage with this market in some way. So there were two different customer jobs that were coming out of SparkToro. One was more focused on service providers and marketing and the other one was more focused on data. And those data purists and those that really wanted verifiable data, well, SparkToro has an advantage on the marketer side more so than on the data analyst side. So that was another thing too. So with that, we made the call to focus on one of those customer jobs.
turns.zh: 还有其他标准。因此，有时您可能希望将一项客户工作优先于另一项工作，如果这些客户以一种非常容易推销的方式聚集在一起。这是一个优势。或者另一个优势，SparkToro 的情况就是这样，就是你在这个市场上以某种方式拥有不公平的优势。 SparkToro 提供了两种不同的客户工作。一种更关注服务提供商和营销，另一种更关注数据。对于那些数据纯粹主义者和那些真正想要可验证数据的人来说，SparkToro 在营销人员方面比在数据分析师方面更有优势。所以那也是另一回事了。因此，我们决定重点关注其中一项客户工作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Can I ask a question here?
turns.zh: 我可以在这里提问吗？

turns.speaker: Georgiana Laudi
turns.en: Yeah, go.
turns.zh: 是啊，走吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So there's two parts of this. There's figuring out who you're going to go after and then what problem you're solving for them. Which do you think is more important at this point? Because step one in this process, just to zoom out a little bit, is figure out your customer and what their problems are so that you can actually solve them well. Do you start with here's who we're going to go after and then here's the biggest problem? How do you think about that?
turns.zh: 所以这有两个部分。弄清楚你要去找谁，然后为他们解决什么问题。您认为此时此刻哪个更重要？因为这个过程的第一步，只是稍微缩小一点，就是弄清楚你的客户以及他们的问题是什么，这样你才能真正很好地解决它们。你是否从我们要追捕的人开始，然后这是最大的问题？您对此有何看法？

turns.speaker: Georgiana Laudi
turns.en: They're sort of one in the same. So because we learned from SparkToro's ideal customers, we already know that they're a fit for the product. They're happy, happily paying, prime them out of their golden hands customers. They're the customers that we want more of. So we've already validated that there's a demand from that customer base. Now, what I'm describing about choosing between two different customer jobs is really just, of those ideal customers, which customer job do you want to lean into? It's not that you wouldn't necessarily still be able to solve for that other customer job, it's just not the one that you would lead with. And I always cautious around this too because sometimes with founders, what'll happen is, there's a level set that just because we were prioritizing one customer job in the short term, doesn't mean you can't serve that other customer job down the line.
turns.zh: 他们是同一个人。因此，由于我们从 SparkToro 的理想客户那里了解到，我们已经知道他们适合该产品。他们很高兴，很乐意付钱，把他们从金手客户手中抢走。他们是我们想要更多的客户。因此，我们已经验证了该客户群的需求。现在，我所描述的关于在两个不同的客户工作之间进行选择的内容实际上只是，在那些理想的客户中，您想倾向于哪一个客户工作？这并不是说您不一定仍然能够解决其他客户的工作，只是这不是您将领导的工作。我对此也总是持谨慎态度，因为有时对于创始人来说，会发生的情况是，有一个水平设定，仅仅因为我们在短期内优先考虑一项客户工作，并不意味着你不能为其他客户工作提供服务。

turns.speaker: Georgiana Laudi
turns.en: A classic example of that is products that serve both brands and agencies for example. So the customer job for brands will be slightly different than agencies. And if you've got an advantage with one, you would just start with one and then you would go back after it. That's a bit of a level up after the fact. It's not part of the core processes, it's what you would do after. But it doesn't mean you can't solve for the other customer jobs, it just means put one foot in front of the other, do a really good job of one thing first, and then we'll add that on later. I don't know if that a hundred percent answered your question though.
turns.zh: 一个典型的例子是为品牌和代理商提供服务的产品。因此，品牌的客户工作将与代理商略有不同。如果你在其中一项上有优势，你就会从一项开始，然后再回去。事后看来，这个水平有点高了。它不是核心流程的一部分，而是您之后要做的事情。但这并不意味着你不能解决其他客户的工作，它只是意味着先把一只脚放在另一只脚前面，先把一件事做好，然后我们会在稍后添加它。我不知道这是否百分百回答了你的问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。是的。

turns.speaker: Georgiana Laudi
turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The reason that you start here is... Basically what you're trying to do is help SparkToro, in this example, grow faster.
turns.zh: 您从这里开始的原因是...基本上，您想要做的是帮助 SparkToro（在本例中）更快地成长。

turns.speaker: Georgiana Laudi
turns.en: I mean we're trying to help them figure out why they're free-to-paid conversion rate was lower than what they wanted. Right? That was the challenge they came to us with. Our traffic numbers are good. Even our signups on our website, our positioning and messaging on our website is clearly doing a good job. But once people get into the product, there's not enough of them getting to value quickly enough. I mean they still had healthy customer base, but they knew that that number could be increased. So we knew what we were solving for.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，我们正在努力帮助他们弄清楚为什么免费到付费的转化率低于他们想要的。正确的？这就是他们给我们带来的挑战。我们的客流量很好。即使我们在网站上的注册、我们网站上的定位和消息传递显然都做得很好。但一旦人们开始使用该产品，就没有足够多的人足够快地获得价值。我的意思是他们仍然拥有健康的客户群，但他们知道这个数字可以增加。所以我们知道我们要解决什么问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. Okay. That helps.
turns.zh: 知道了。好的。这有帮助。

turns.speaker: Georgiana Laudi
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So step one here is figure out who do you want to focus on, not just... Because a lot of people would go at this problem like, "Okay, conversion is whatever, 10%, how do we increase? Let's look at this data. Let's look at it. They're bouncing. Let's look at why people are confused." And your approach is, "No, let's focus on the people we really want to get into this product and focus on making them convert, and not focus as much on the general case of conversion."
turns.zh: 因此，第一步是弄清楚你想关注谁，而不仅仅是……因为很多人会在解决这个问题时说，“好吧，转化率是什么，10%，我们如何提高？让我们看看这些数据。让我们看看它。他们正在跳动。让我们看看为什么人们感到困惑。”你的方法是，“不，让我们专注于我们真正想要进入这个产品的人，并专注于让他们转化，而不是过多关注一般的转化情况。”

turns.speaker: Georgiana Laudi
turns.en: Right. We would get to that though. That's a really important part of the process, but it comes after figuring out who you're even solving for. But it's definitely important to look at those numbers. I mean, I'm not saying don't look at the data. Obviously you have to. They wouldn't have identified a problem had they not been looking at the data. So the challenge that happened so, so often, and I mean this happens with a lot of teams, particularly marketers fall victim to this tactical way of approaching things and piecemealing things, piecemealing campaigns or programs to prove that we're doing something and we're driving up numbers, and they don't take big enough sort of swings. So this is like, zoom out for a second, figure out who is it that you even want coming through the front door. I mean, the social media platform tool that I mentioned, the trial-to-pay conversion rate bumped up 40% because a higher qualified person comes through the front door. So it matters.
turns.zh: 正确的。不过我们会做到这一点。这是这个过程中非常重要的一部分，但它是在弄清楚你要为谁解决问题之后进行的。但看看这些数字绝对很重要。我的意思是，我并不是说不要看数据。显然你必须这样做。如果他们没有查看数据，他们就不会发现问题。因此，经常发生的挑战，我的意思是，这种情况发生在很多团队中，尤其是营销人员，他们成为这种处理事情和零碎事情、零碎活动或计划的战术方式的受害者，以证明我们正在做某事并且我们正在提高数字，但他们没有采取足够大的波动。所以这就像，缩小一秒钟，找出你想要从前门进来的人是谁。我的意思是，我提到的社交媒体平台工具，试用到付费的转化率上升了 40%，因为更高素质的人进来了。所以这很重要。

turns.speaker: Georgiana Laudi
turns.en: So if you can zoom out and keep in your mind's eye that ideal customer job, that thing that you're solving for. We're not at personas. We don't care about personas at all. They're important when you start talking about advertising and targeting and that demographic data that you have to know when you're doing advertising and things like that. That is not what I'm describing here at all. I find that jobs be done too helps tie and bond marketing and product and customer success together a lot more because all three of those teams, or arguably four with sales, should all be focused on this theme customer that's not revolutionary. So this is just a sort of helpful way to do that.
turns.zh: 因此，如果您能够缩小范围并牢记理想的客户工作，即您正在解决的问题。我们不是在人物角色。我们根本不关心角色。当您开始谈论广告和定位以及您在做广告和类似事情时必须了解的人口统计数据时，它们很重要。这根本不是我在这里描述的。我发现完成工作也有助于将营销、产品和客户成功更多地联系在一起，因为所有这三个团队，或者可以说是四个销售团队，都应该专注于这个不是革命性的主题客户。所以这只是一种有用的方法。

turns.speaker: Georgiana Laudi
turns.en: Product teams know and subscribe for the most part to the jobs-to-be-done theory. So marketers should follow suit, and there's a lot to be gained anyway on the marketing side. So anyway, the short of it basically is that because we knew we were focused on increasing that free-to-pay conversion rate, the next step after the job is the mapping. So it's identifying, okay, for this ideal customer, what are those key milestones in their relationship with our product? What are those big of leaps of faith is how I describe it. I mean I don't need to explain. The Airbnb customer journey tells that story. Where's a value moment in this relationship? Where are they reaching value?
turns.zh: 产品团队了解并认同“待完成工作”理论。因此营销人员应该效仿，无论如何在营销方面都有很多收获。无论如何，它的缺点基本上是，因为我们知道我们的重点是提高免费到付费的转化率，所以工作之后的下一步就是绘制地图。因此，对于这个理想的客户来说，确定他们与我们产品的关系中的关键里程碑是什么？我是这么描述的，什么是信仰的巨大飞跃。我的意思是我不需要解释。 Airbnb 的客户旅程讲述了这个故事。这段关系的价值时刻在哪里？他们在哪里实现价值？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Make some examples of that for folks that are trying to do this for themselves potentially. And then also, how many of these moments would you suggest people have?
turns.zh: 为那些可能尝试为自己做这件事的人举一些例子。然后，您建议人们有多少这样的时刻？

turns.speaker: Georgiana Laudi
turns.en: Yeah. So it completely depends on the product and the customer for that matter. I shouldn't leave that part over it. Obviously that's important. In general though, what we would do is, we'd break it down into a struggle phase and evaluation phase and a growth phase. Struggle phase is, they're experiencing the problem, life sucks, they're using the old way, something's got to happen, they've got to solve this thing. In general, the struggle phase would break down between out in the world experiencing the problem for the first time. So we call that a problem. And generally there would be another one called interest, where it's like, "Okay, now they're starting to shop around. They're getting into solution seeking mode." They might be on your website. They might be on your competitor's websites. They're reading product reviews, things like that. That's interest stage.
turns.zh: 是的。因此，这完全取决于产品和客户。我不应该把那部分留在上面。显然这很重要。但总的来说，我们要做的是，将其分为奋斗阶段、评估阶段和成长阶段。挣扎阶段是，他们正在经历问题，生活很糟糕，他们正在使用旧的方式，一定会发生一些事情，他们必须解决这个问题。一般来说，斗争阶段会在第一次遇到这个问题的人之间结束。所以我们称之为问题。一般来说，还有另一种叫做兴趣，就像，“好吧，现在他们开始货比三家。他们正在进入寻求解决方案的模式。”它们可能在您的网站上。它们可能位于您竞争对手的网站上。他们正在阅读产品评论之类的东西。这就是兴趣阶段。

turns.speaker: Georgiana Laudi
turns.en: And then there's the evaluation phase, which generally breaks down, I will say two or three milestones within the evaluation phase. I say two or three because if you have a more complex product, more complex customer is the more likely scenario. There may be more leaps of faith or more milestones, heavier lift for you to take. So we have worked with companies where the evaluation phase has been three or four milestones, I would always default to as few as possible. So if I'm cutting it down to lowest common denominator, I would say a first value would be the first milestone within evaluation. So you want to get them to that product activation really, really quickly. And then value realization is the milestone where you're solving that customer job. So they reach a point with your product where they're like, "Hell yes, this is it." And for the first time, they reach this critical threshold of product engagement. Now, what that product engagement is with your unique product for that specific customer is up for debate, but there still needs to be that moment.
turns.zh: 然后是评估阶段，通常会崩溃，我会说评估阶段内有两个或三个里程碑。我说两个或三个是因为如果你有更复杂的产品，更可能出现更复杂的客户。可能会有更多的信念飞跃或更多的里程碑，需要你承担更重的提升。因此，我们与评估阶段具有三四个里程碑的公司合作，我总是默认尽可能少的里程碑。因此，如果我将其减少到最低公分母，我会说第一个值将是评估中的第一个里程碑。所以你想让他们非常非常快地激活产品。然后价值实现就是您解决客户工作的里程碑。因此，他们对你的产品达到了一个临界点，他们会说，“天啊，是的，就是这样。”他们第一次达到了产品参与度的这一关键门槛。现在，针对特定客户的独特产品的产品参与度尚有争议，但仍然需要那个时刻。

turns.speaker: Georgiana Laudi
turns.en: And then there's the growth phase, which is about the continued value. So getting to frequency of usage and a healthy building of that habit, getting into a cadence that makes sense. What type of feature usage and end product usage should you want to see there and then on what frequency becomes really important. And then there's another milestone generally after that where you're like, "Okay cool, they're in. They're pro. Now, what else do they need?" What else do they need from a product? And also, how else can we amplify them or work with them to either start teaching our tool to other people? I mean there's all kinds of things that can happen about growth. That's where the promise that exponential growth assess sort of comes into play.
turns.zh: 然后是增长阶段，即持续价值。因此，了解使用频率并健康地养成这种习惯，进入有意义的节奏。您希望在那里看到什么类型的功能使用情况和最终产品使用情况以及什么频率变得非常重要。然后通常还有另一个里程碑，你会想，“好吧，酷，他们进来了。他们是职业选手。现在，他们还需要什么？”他们还需要从产品中得到什么？而且，我们还能如何扩大它们或与它们合作，开始向其他人教授我们的工具？我的意思是，成长过程中可能会发生各种各样的事情。这就是指数增长评估的承诺发挥作用的地方。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And as people listen to this, just to maybe help if it's not super obvious, what people shouldn't imagine is like a little key frame, a storyboard frame of like, "Here's something your customer is doing." Right?
turns.zh: 当人们听到这个时，如果它不是非常明显的话，也许只是为了提供帮助，人们不应该想象像一个小关键帧，一个故事板框架，“这是你的客户正在做的事情。”正确的？

turns.speaker: Georgiana Laudi
turns.en: Yeah. We often talk about it and describe it as the story of how I met and fell in love with your product. It's like this documentary of being out in the world, finding it, realizing that like, "Hell yeah, this might actually solve a problem for us. This might be it." Getting that enough value to convince them to keep going to full value realization, to continue value-to-value growth.
turns.zh: 是的。我们经常谈论它，并将其描述为我如何遇见并爱上你们产品的故事。就像一部纪录片，讲述的是走出去的世界，发现它，意识到，“天哪，这实际上可能为我们解决一个问题。也许就是这样。”获得足够的价值来说服他们继续全面实现价值，继续实现价值增长。

turns.speaker: Lenny

Maven is a cohort-based learning platform where you learn alongside peers with a direct connection to your instructor. Maven got a ton of courses for product managers, founders, and executives to help them level up in all kinds of ways. Over 10,000 people from Airbnb to Coinbase to Google to Tesla have taken courses from real experts and operators that have spent decades honing their craft.
turns.zh: 本集由 Maven 为您带来。从第一天起，我就是 Maven 的投资者、顾问和客户。我什至通过 Maven 教授我的产品管理课程。 Maven 是一个基于队列的学习平台，您可以与同伴一起学习，并直接与讲师联系。 Maven 为产品经理、创始人和高管提供了大量课程，帮助他们以各种方式提升水平。从 Airbnb 到 Coinbase，从 Google 到 Tesla，超过 10,000 名员工已经接受了真正的专家和运营商的课程，他们花了几十年的时间磨练自己的技术。
